transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-02 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Jasmine (Redwood AE), Marco (Redwood SE), Ellen (DriftWood CTO), Samir (Lead ML Eng), Priya (Security)
Shared artifacts: short deck https://redwood.example/deck/driftwood-intro, benchmark template (shared link in chat)

[00:00] Jasmine: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, I'm Jasmine on the Redwood AE side, Marco is our solutions engineer, we'll run through requirements and then get into models, deployment options.
[00:18] Ellen: Thanks, yeah I'm Ellen, CTO at DriftWood. We're evaluating options for customer-facing assistant across support and admin flows. Key bits are 32k tokens for long policy context and multilingual support — english, spanish, french, maybe chinese later.
[00:33] Samir: And hi, Samir here. We're running models in-house currently but looking to offload inference because our ops team is burning cycles. Also need tool-calling to hit our backend APIs for ticket triage.
[00:46] Priya: Priya, security. I'll be focused on SSO, audit logs, KMS, and data residency.
[00:54] Marco: Great, thanks. quick clarification: when you say 32k context, is that peak or steady-state? any idea about distribution?
[01:05] Ellen: Peak. Most sessions are 2-4k tokens but occasionally we ingest full customer history + attachments and push near 30k. Need tail support more than full-time.
[01:16] Marco: Understood. That drives model choice and hosting. For open models, we usually compare Mistral/InternLM/Guanaco variants or custom finetuned Llama forks. For 32k we recommend models that have native long-context or can be segmented with KV cache — helps with latency + cost.
[01:35] Samir: We looked at the guan-32k fork, but our perf tests on our infra show memory blowouts. how does Redwood manage long KV cache?
[01:45] Marco: Our runtime keeps a sharded KV cache in GPU memory and can spill to local NVMe when needed, and we do continuous batching. The important bit is kernel selection — smaller attention kernels for long context. There will be a latency vs cost tradeoff if you want strict p99 < 400ms on 32k.
[02:02] Ellen: p99 400ms is our target for small replies, but for long summary ops we can accept higher. We can't have constant 2s latency on UI though.
[02:12] Jasmine: That's helpful. question on deployment mode: are you leaning Hosted, Dedicated reserved, or Private?
[02:20] Ellen: Prefer hosted for speed of rollout, but security asks may push us to Dedicated or Private. For EU customers we need data residency.
[02:29] Priya: We need logs retained for 2 years, SOC 2, SSO (SAML), and KMS integration. If Hosted can meet those via customer-owned keys and region isolation, it's acceptable.
[02:42] Marco: We can do Hosted with customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest, per-token tracing in the console, and region routing. For stricter isolation we recommend Dedicated or Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem). Dedicated gives predictable latency and an isolated GPU pool.
[02:57] Samir: Cost question — for Dedicated what's the baseline? we have an estimate of 8 GPUs for peak concurrency.
[03:05] Jasmine: We'll produce a detailed estimate, but rough math: Dedicated monthly commit starts at X depending on GPU class. We'll include amortized token costs and expected batch gains. Also our Optimize tooling can recommend quantization + batching to reduce unit cost.
[03:22] Ellen: On multilingual quality — we've seen regressions when switching quantized weights for non-English. Any guidance?
[03:28] Marco: Good point. Quantization can sometimes reduce quality in low-resource languages. We recommend a small eval set per language; Redwood Optimize can run regression checks across your prompt set and track quality delta. For some languages you might pick a larger float model or keep higher-precision kernels for generation.
[03:48] Samir: For tool-calling, we need structured output: call ticket_create(api) with JSON payload. Does Redwood support function/tool calling with hooks to auth?
[03:58] Marco: Yes — we support tool-calling primitives in the hosted API and also server-side tool adapters for Private/Dedicated. You can register a tool schema and we pass back structured outputs. For security we support signed tool calls, and you can proxy through your own service in VPC.
[04:15] Priya: If tool-calls are proxied, we need mutual TLS and audit trails. Does Redwood provide per-call trace IDs?
[04:23] Marco: Yes, per-request tracing, exportable to your tracing backend. Audit logs include request metadata and which model/version served the call.
[04:31] Ellen: Let's dig into model choices. show us recommended candidate list for long context, good multilingual support, and open license.
[04:40] Marco: Candidate list off the top: 1) OpenLlama-65B with LORA finetune and 32k context patch, 2) Guanaco-33k variant (community forks), 3) Mistral long-context derivatives, 4) LlamaX 70B-long. We also sometimes present a hybrid: use a smaller fast model for short queries and fallback to long-context model for heavy requests — smart routing.
[05:05] Samir: Smart routing interest — can we route by token length or cost threshold?
[05:10] Marco: Absolutely. Policy-based routing: by length, by customer tier, or by estimated cost. You can set automatic fallbacks.
[05:16] Jasmine: Example: short assistant replies go to a 7B quantized model on Hosted, and long document actions route to a Dedicated long-context 33B. That saves tokens and keeps p50 latency low.
[05:28] Ellen: Nice. question about rollouts — can we canary a model change just for subset of users?
[05:34] Marco: Yes canary and A/B rollouts are in Redwood Console. You can also tie eval regressions to prompt sets and auto rollback on quality regressions.
[05:45] Priya: Data retention: how do we handle logs for EU-only customers?
[05:51] Marco: Region routing to EU regions plus retention policies per workspace. For Hosted we can pin data to a region, and for Private we can keep everything on-prem.
[06:00] Samir: Performance: can you share real-world numbers for 32k with 33B models?
[06:06] Marco: We'll share benchmark sheet. Roughly, with continuous KV caching and optimized kernels, p50 might be sub-300ms for short replies, but full 32k compress + summarize ops will be in the 1.2-2s range depending on GPU. We'll include token/sec numbers per GPU in the spreadsheet.
[06:24] Ellen: Ok, that's consistent with our expectations. next, integration: we need SDKs for node and python.
[06:30] Jasmine: We have official SDKs, examples for tool-calling and streaming, and quickstart templates. We'll drop links.
[06:37] Priya: About compliance docs — do you support bringing your own audit logs to our SIEM?
[06:42] Marco: Yes logs can be shipped to your SIEM via push or pulled from our export. We also support syslog and cloud-native exporters.
[06:50] Ellen: Let's talk timeline. We want a pilot in prod-ish traffic by end of Q3. Ideally start pilot in June with 4-week evaluation.
[06:58] Jasmine: Sounds good. Proposed pilot: 1) baseline perf run (using your test prompts) 2) hosted pilot with customer-managed KMS and EU routing 3) evaluate accuracy/cost and then scope Dedicated if needed.
[07:12] Samir: We'll provide a dataset and example prompts. how much data do you need for evaluation?
[07:16] Marco: A representative prompt set, 500-1,000 examples across long and short flows, and ground truth labels for classification/regression items. For multilingual, at least 50 examples per language to flag regressions.
[07:29] Priya: We'll need to review the contract around data usage and deletion SLAs.
[07:33] Jasmine: We'll send the legal addendum and SOC 2 paperwork.
[07:38] Ellen: ok wrapping up, quick recap?
[07:41] Jasmine: Recap: Marco to run 32k and 64k perf/cost numbers and share benchmark spreadsheet; Jasmine to send SOC2/SSO/KMS docs plus pricing for Dedicated and Hosted pilot; Priya to share compliance checklist and residency needs; schedule pilot kickoff for week of 2027-06-14.
[07:58] Ellen: Good. any blockers?
[08:01] Priya: None immediate, just need the paperwork.
[08:04] Samir: I'll assemble prompt set this week.
[08:07] Jasmine: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links.

[08:20] End meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: some names transcribed as 'Guan-32' or 'LamaX' — please refer to provided model list in the deck.
